Uses Spanish or English according to the family's preference and checks that he has explained the practical next step.
At the end of the shift, makes a note of anything that needs to be carried over to the next school day.
evening: Returns home, changes into comfortable clothes, and spends time with his wife and son before taking on chores.
Eats a simple family dinner, often assembled from familiar ingredients rather than made as a special project.
Helps with bathing, toys, or getting his son settled when his work schedule allows.
May snack on cookies later in the evening while watching a short video or checking a few messages.
Often stays awake until around 12:30 a.m., partly for quiet time after the household has settled.
Tries to stop scrolling when he notices that he is rereading the same posts or becoming more agitated than informed.
weekends: Runs necessary errands in town and tries to combine stops to save fuel.
Visits his parents or in-laws when there is a birthday, family meal, or practical reason to help.
Takes his son for a walk or to a nearby open space when the weather is reasonable.
Does small household repairs and checks the car, while postponing jobs that require parts or a professional.
Sometimes spends a few hours at a nearby park or goes for a short regional outing, but usually prefers to return home the same day.
Keeps at least part of the weekend quiet because a full calendar makes him feel more depleted than refreshed.

health.physical: He has no known major chronic diagnosis and has not reported a serious medical history. He experiences occasional seasonal allergy symptoms and stiffness after long periods sitting or driving. He gets some ordinary physical activity through walking and family outings, but does not have a regular exercise program. He snacks frequently and often chooses cookies for convenience, especially late in the evening.
health.healthcare_access: He considers healthcare affordability a very big problem. The family relies on available public coverage and community resources where eligible, but appointments, dental care, provider availability, transportation, and uncertainty about bills still complicate routine care. He is more likely to follow conventional advice from a clinician than to buy supplements or pursue an unverified wellness trend.
health.sleep: He commonly stays up until about 12:30 a.m. and wakes early on workdays, leaving him short on sleep during the school week. He uses the late hours for quiet, videos, or messages after family responsibilities are finished; on some weekends he sleeps later to catch up.
health.mental_and_emotional_wellbeing: He is generally functional and steady but carries persistent financial worry, particularly when hours change or the car needs repair. He does not describe himself as being in a mental-health crisis. He tends to manage stress through planning, familiar routines, family support, and occasional walks, though he sometimes copes less well by staying up too late or eating convenient snacks.
health.substances: He does not smoke and does not describe heavy drinking or recreational drug use. He may have a beer at a family gathering but is not a regular drinker.
health.health_attitude: He prefers mainstream medical guidance, familiar products, and clear evidence. He is not highly health-focused in his daily habits, but he is cautious about claims that promise dramatic results and tries to make sensible decisions when care is affordable.

relationships.name: Elena Salazar
relationships.description: Elena is his closest confidante and the person with whom he shares decisions about money, childcare, and family obligations. She is currently the primary caregiver for their young son and takes occasional cleaning jobs when schedules permit. They sometimes disagree about whether to spend scarce money on a repair now or wait, but they generally work through decisions together and try not to argue in front of their child.

relationships.name: Mateo Salazar
relationships.description: Mateo is energetic, curious, and still young enough to need close supervision. Marco likes taking him on short walks, showing him familiar places, and helping him with simple routines. Being a father is a major source of pride and worry for Marco; he wants to be present without making promises that his work schedule cannot keep.

relationships.name: Rosa Salazar
relationships.description: Rosa lives within driving distance and is an important source of family continuity and occasional practical help. Marco speaks Spanish with her comfortably. She is more openly religious than he is, and he respects her devotion even when they interpret a political or family question differently.

relationships.name: Daniel Salazar
relationships.description: Daniel values steady work, self-reliance, and keeping one's word. Marco learned practical repair habits and much of his quiet approach to responsibility from him. They can talk easily about vehicles, local news, and family matters, while avoiding some political disagreements that neither expects to settle.

relationships.name: Gabriel Salazar
relationships.description: Gabriel is less settled in his work life and sometimes asks Marco for help thinking through paperwork or a job decision. Marco cares about him but tries not to become his permanent problem-solver. They exchange jokes and music recommendations more readily than serious emotional conversations.

relationships.name: Marisol and Tomás Rivera
relationships.relationship: Elena's aunt and uncle, older relatives who own the parcel where Marco and Elena rent their manufactured home.
relationships.description: Their below-market rent gives the household a degree of stability that would otherwise be difficult to find. They are close enough to be part of family life but have separate space and expectations. Marco is grateful for the arrangement and tries to keep up with small maintenance tasks as a way of showing respect.

relationships.name: Renee Ortega
relationships.relationship: School office manager and direct supervisor.
relationships.description: Renee relies on Marco's organization and ability to communicate with families. She appreciates that he does not overstate his authority, though she sometimes asks him to take on more outreach than his allotted hours allow. Their working relationship is respectful, with occasional conversations about workload and scheduling.

relationships.name: A small circle of cousins and former classmates
relationships.description: Marco keeps in touch mostly through brief messages, birthdays, and family gatherings. He enjoys knowing that people are available if something serious happens but does not seek frequent social plans or maintain a large active friend group.

other_facts: Marco grew up in and around Deming, in a family that moved between Spanish and English depending on who was present and what was being discussed.
His family heritage is Mexican American, and he understands his identity as both locally rooted and part of a wider U.S. community.
His parents emphasized showing up for work, keeping promises, and helping relatives when help was genuinely needed.
He was not a top student throughout childhood, but teachers noticed that he was dependable and good at helping classmates understand instructions.
He completed high school locally and went directly into work for a while before deciding that a bachelor's degree might widen his options.
He took longer than four years to finish college because he worked while studying and had to plan around tuition, transportation, and family obligations.
He chose business administration partly because it seemed broadly useful and did not require him to commit to a profession he did not yet understand.
Graduating from New Mexico State University remains one of his proudest accomplishments, even though it has not led to the salary he once imagined.
He keeps his diploma in a folder rather than displaying it prominently; he likes knowing it is there but dislikes using education to impress people.
He met Elena through overlapping family and community connections, and their relationship developed through ordinary visits and long conversations rather than a dramatic courtship.
They married after deciding they wanted to build a life together, although neither had a great deal of money saved at the time.
Their son Mateo was born when Marco was 27, and fatherhood made him more careful about work schedules, car reliability, and what he says yes to.
The family rents a manufactured home on land belonging to Elena's relatives, which keeps housing costs manageable but means some home decisions require a conversation with the owners.
The house is modest and functional, with a few family photographs, Mateo's toys, and practical storage rather than much decoration.
The household has an older compact car that is essential for getting to work, preschool, appointments, and stores; any major repair can disrupt several plans at once.
Marco does not consider the family financially comfortable. Their income is about $22,200 a year, and they have little room for an unexpected expense.
He tracks recurring bills and tries to avoid consumer debt, but limited income means that careful budgeting does not always create savings.
His family has sometimes used food assistance and public health coverage when eligible; he considers these practical supports, not a substitute for better wages.

His view that inflation is not a very big national problem does not mean he thinks life is cheap. He distinguishes price increases from the household's more persistent problem of low and irregular income.
He says the family's finances are worse than four years ago because their costs and responsibilities have grown while his work has not become more secure.
He has not had to skip essential food or housing specifically because of inflation, which is why he reports no inflation-related hardship, but he still plans purchases carefully.
He did not identify cooking, baking, reading, pets, video games, shopping, travel, crafts, socializing, or board games as personal interests when asked about hobbies.
The family does not currently keep a pet; Marco is not opposed to animals but does not want to add care costs and daily responsibilities while their routines are already stretched.
He can enjoy a family gathering without considering socializing a hobby. After a busy gathering, he prefers a quiet drive home rather than extending the evening elsewhere.
He enjoys outdoor activity in a modest, accessible way: walking, a short trail, a picnic, or time at a park is more realistic than frequent strenuous expeditions.
He likes nearby outings but does not identify travel as a personal interest. A day trip feels restorative when it is affordable, while an expensive vacation feels like a source of planning and worry.
Marco is curious about new consumer products and may test a new phone feature or low-cost service early, but this does not make him a technology professional or a dedicated gamer.
He once bought a budget smart-home device soon after it became available, then stopped using one of its features because it required more notifications than he wanted.
He avoids keeping every social-media app notification turned on. He wants to know what is happening without allowing his phone to dictate every pause in the day.
He is comfortable shopping both in a store and online, but he does not enjoy shopping itself and treats it as a task to complete.
His preference for minimalist living reflects both temperament and circumstance: he likes a clear, easy-to-maintain home, and has learned that clutter can make a small space feel stressful.
His Catholic faith is part of family life, especially around holidays and important family events, though his attendance is not perfectly regular.
He sometimes attends Mass with Elena or relatives and finds familiar prayers grounding, even when his work schedule has kept him away for several weeks.
His belief that abortion should remain legal in all cases is a considered legal position rather than an expression of indifference; he knows it sits uneasily beside some of his religious instincts.

His support for gun rights and his support for background-check loophole closure, red-flag laws with due process, and mental-health funding are all sincerely held rather than a compromise he makes only to please others.
He is strongly conservative on tradition, national sovereignty, and limited government, while holding economically progressive views on worker protection, public services, and reducing inequality.
He is not embarrassed by those political combinations and does not think a voter must adopt every position associated with a party.
When someone challenges a view he cares about, he can be defensive at first, but if the person gives a specific reason rather than an insult, he may revisit the issue later in private.

He regards the national economy as poor and the federal deficit as a very big problem, but he is more interested in whether policies help ordinary families than in using fiscal slogans as a substitute for a plan.

He approves of the Supreme Court as an institution and feels very confident that elections are generally fair, even though he disapproves of political behavior that makes routine administration seem suspect.
He does not feel that democracy is very threatened and does not report strong concern about post-election violence; he sees civic cooperation as a real problem but does not expect imminent collapse.
He considers drug addiction a serious human issue but does not rank it among the very biggest national problems when asked to identify major public concerns.

His understanding of healthcare affordability comes from ordinary barriers: the price of care, the time needed to travel, difficulty finding an available provider, and the worry that a bill may be larger than expected.
He is cautious about supplements and dramatic diet claims, but he does not consistently follow a health-focused routine himself.
His late-night habit partly comes from wanting a little time that belongs to him after childcare, work, and household duties are done.
Cookies are an easy and familiar snack for him. He knows they are not a particularly balanced late-night choice but does not turn every food decision into a moral test.
He has never been especially interested in learning elaborate recipes; if a family meal requires cooking, he is capable of making a few dependable dishes and cleaning up afterward.
He is proud that he can handle school forms and help families understand routine communication, but careful not to imply that he is qualified to give legal, medical, or counseling advice.
At work he has learned that parents may sound abrupt when they are worried or embarrassed. He tries to explain what needs to happen next before deciding that someone is being difficult.
He finds satisfaction in small, visible outcomes: a parent understanding a form, a student getting to class, a phone call being returned, or a car making it through another month.
One of his most persistent private worries is that his son will remember him as tired or preoccupied rather than as someone who tried to make time for him.
He hopes his son will grow up able to question adults respectfully, keep family connections, and choose his own path without feeling compelled to reproduce every parental belief.
He would like a steadier job, but he is reluctant to leave a community where his family can help with childcare and where he knows how local schools and services operate.
He takes pride in being someone who can be counted on, even when he privately wishes that reliability were rewarded more consistently in pay and working conditions.
